Implement `packSlots(items, slotSize)` in src/slot-pack.js, as a named export. The stub in that file shows the shape, and test/slot-pack.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

Rules:
R1. `items` is an array of `{ id, size }`, where `id` is a string and `size` is a positive integer. `slotSize` is a positive integer. An item whose `size` equals `slotSize` fits exactly.
R2. Items are placed in order of decreasing `size`. Items of equal `size` are placed in ascending `id` order (compared as strings with `<`).
R3. Each item goes into the first existing slot, in creation order, that still has enough room. If no slot has, a new slot is created for it and it goes there.
R4. The result is an array of slots in creation order. Each slot is an array of item ids in the order the items were placed into it.
R5. An item whose `size` is greater than `slotSize` makes the function throw a `RangeError` whose message contains that item's `id`. If several items are too large, the message names the first one in placement order (R2) and no other.
R6. The input array and its items are not modified.
R7. An empty `items` array gives `[]`.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

Implement `encodeTicket({ venue, row, seat })` and `decodeTicket(code)` in src/ticket-code.js, as named exports. The stubs in that file show the shapes, and test/ticket-code.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

Rules:
R1. `venue` is an integer from 1 to 99, `row` an integer of 1 or more, and `seat` an integer from 1 to 999. Anything else (including a non-integer or a string) makes `encodeTicket` throw a `RangeError`.
R2. A code looks like `V07-AB-012-G`: the letter `V`, the venue as two digits, `-`, the row label, `-`, the seat as three digits, `-`, and one check letter.
R3. The row label is the row number in bijective base 26 with the letters A to Z: row 1 is `A`, row 26 is `Z`, row 27 is `AA`, row 52 is `AZ`, row 53 is `BA`, row 702 is `ZZ`, and row 703 is `AAA`.
R4. The check letter is computed from the text before the last `-` (for the code above, `V07-AB-012`): add up the character codes (`charCodeAt`) of every character of that text, take the sum modulo 23, and use the result as an index into the string `ACDEFGHJKLMNPQRSTUVWXYZ`. For example `V07-AB-012` gives `G`, and `V01-A-001` gives `A`.
R5. `decodeTicket(code)` returns `{ venue, row, seat }` as numbers, and is the exact inverse of `encodeTicket` for every valid ticket.
R6. `decodeTicket` throws a `SyntaxError` if its argument is not a string of exactly the form in R2 (a lowercase letter anywhere, the wrong number of digits, an empty or non-letter row label, a missing or extra part). It throws a `RangeError` if the form is right but the venue is `00`, the seat is `000`, or the check letter is wrong.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

Implement the class `RollingMedian` in src/rolling-median.js, as a named export. The stub in that file shows the methods, and test/rolling-median.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

Rules:
R1. `new RollingMedian(windowSize)` requires `windowSize` to be an integer of 1 or more; anything else throws a `RangeError`.
R2. `add(x)` requires `x` to be a finite number (not NaN, not an infinity, not a numeric string) and throws a `TypeError` otherwise, leaving the window unchanged. A valid `x` goes in as the newest value; if the window now holds more than `windowSize` values, the oldest value is dropped. `add` returns the median of the window after that.
R3. The median of the window is the middle value after sorting ascending. When the window holds an even number of values, it is the lower of the two middle values (not their average). `median()` returns the same thing at any time, and returns `null` when the window is empty.
R4. The getter `size` is the number of values currently in the window. `values()` returns a new array of the values from oldest to newest; changing that array does not change the window.
R5. `reset()` empties the window and returns `undefined`. The window size is kept.
R6. `resize(n)` sets a new window size, with the same check as R1. If the window holds more than `n` values it drops the oldest ones until it holds `n`. It returns the median after resizing (`null` if empty). Later calls to `add` use the new size.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

Implement `findConflicts(bookings)` in src/booking-conflicts.js, as a named export. The stub in that file shows the shape, and test/booking-conflicts.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

A booking is `{ id, room, start, end }`.

Rules:
R1. `bookings` must be an array, and every booking needs a non-empty string `id`, a non-empty string `room`, and `start` and `end` strings of exactly the form `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ` that name a real calendar moment (`2026-02-30T10:00:00Z` does not). Otherwise `findConflicts` throws a `TypeError`.
R2. A booking whose `end` is not after its `start` makes `findConflicts` throw a `RangeError`. Two bookings with the same `id` make it throw a `TypeError`.
R3. The bookings are checked one at a time in array order, and the first problem found is the one thrown. For each booking the order is: R1 for that booking, then R2's `end` check, then R2's duplicate-`id` check against the bookings before it.
R4. Two bookings conflict when they have the same `room` (room names are case-sensitive: `A1` and `a1` are different rooms) and their time ranges overlap. A range runs from `start` up to but not including `end`, so a booking that ends at the moment another one starts does not conflict with it. Identical ranges conflict, and so does a range inside another.
R5. The result is an array of `[idA, idB]` pairs, one for each conflicting pair of bookings, with `idA < idB` in the usual string comparison (`<`). The pairs are sorted by `idA`, then by `idB`. No bookings, or no conflicts, gives `[]`.
R6. `findConflicts` does not change the array it is given or the bookings in it.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

Implement `render(text)` in src/markup-lite.js, as a named export. The stub in that file shows the shape, and test/markup-lite.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/. `render` turns a small markup language into an HTML string. Rules: R1. `render` throws a `TypeError` if `text` is not a string. In the output, `&`, `<` and `>` become `&`, `<` and `>` everywhere, including inside code. Every other character (quotes, newlines, anything else) is copied unchanged. R2. `*x*` becomes `x`, `_x_` becomes `x`, and `` `x` `` becomes `x`. R3. A `*` or `_` opens a span only if the character right after it exists and is not whitespace. Its closer is the first later marker of the same kind whose previous character is not whitespace, and which is not the character immediately after the opener (the content must not be empty). A marker with no closer is plain text, and so is an opener that is not allowed to open. R4. `_` has an extra condition: it opens only if the character before it is the start of the text or is not a letter or digit (`A`-`Z`, `a`-`z`, `0`-`9`), and it closes only if the character after it is the end of the text or is not a letter or digit. So `snake_case_name` is plain text. `*` has no such condition. R5. A backtick opens a code span that ends at the next backtick. Inside it only R1's escaping applies: no markup, and no backslash handling. A backtick with no later backtick is plain text. Two backticks next to each other with nothing between are plain text, as two backticks. Code spans take priority: when looking for the closer of a `*` or `_` span, a complete code span is skipped over, so a marker inside it can never be the closer. R6. The content of a `*` or `_` span is rendered by the same rules (for example `*a _b_ c*` becomes `a b c`). A span ends at its first valid closer, so spans never overlap: in `*a _b* c_` the bold span holds `a _b`, where the `_` has no closer inside the span and so is plain text. R7. A backslash followed by `*`, `_`, a backtick or another backslash outputs that second character as plain text (the backslash is dropped), and that character is not a marker and is never a closer. A backslash anywhere else, and any backslash inside a code span, is plain text. When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

Implement `computeTax(incomeCents, schedule)` in src/tax-brackets.js, as a named export. The stub in that file shows the shape, and test/tax-brackets.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

Rules:
R1. `incomeCents` must be a non-negative integer, otherwise `computeTax` throws a `RangeError`. `schedule` must be a non-empty array of brackets `{ upTo, rateBp }`, otherwise it throws a `TypeError`. `upTo` is a positive integer number of cents, or `null` for the last bracket (no limit), and `rateBp` is an integer from 0 to 10000 (basis points: 2500 is 25%).
R2. A schedule is valid only if its `upTo` values strictly increase, only the last bracket has `upTo: null`, and the last bracket does have `upTo: null`. An invalid schedule throws a `TypeError`. R1 and R2 are both checked before any tax is computed, the schedule first, then `incomeCents`.
R3. The tax is progressive. The first bracket applies to income from 0 up to its `upTo`, each next bracket to the income above the previous `upTo` up to its own `upTo`, and the last to everything above. The tax on the part of the income in a bracket is that part times `rateBp` divided by 10000.
R4. The tax of each bracket is rounded to a whole number of cents on its own, before the brackets are added up, to the nearest cent, and exactly half a cent rounds to the even cent (so 2.5 becomes 2, 3.5 becomes 4, 0.5 becomes 0).
R5. `computeTax` returns an object `{ totalCents, perBracket }`. `perBracket` has one entry per bracket in schedule order, each `{ upTo, rateBp, taxableCents, taxCents }`, where `taxableCents` is the part of the income in that bracket (0 for brackets the income does not reach), and `totalCents` is the sum of the `taxCents` values.
R6. `computeTax` does not change `schedule` or the brackets in it, and it uses exact integer arithmetic: results must be right for incomes up to 9007199254740991 / 10000 cents with no floating-point error.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

Implement `normalizeRoute(path)` in src/route-normalize.js, as a named export. The stub in that file shows the shape, and test/route-normalize.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

Rules:
R1. `path` must be a string that starts with `/` and contains no `?` and no `#`; otherwise `normalizeRoute` throws a `TypeError`.
R2. Percent escapes are decoded first, before anything else in these rules. A `%` that is not followed by two hexadecimal digits makes `normalizeRoute` throw a `SyntaxError`. A valid escape `%XX` whose character is unreserved (a letter `A`-`Z` or `a`-`z`, a digit, or one of `-` `.` `_` `~`) is replaced by that character. Any other valid escape stays an escape, with its two hex digits in upper case (`%2f` becomes `%2F`, and it is not a path separator).
R3. Repeated slashes count as one slash.
R4. A segment that is exactly `.` is removed. A segment that is exactly `..` is removed together with the segment before it. A `..` with no segment before it makes `normalizeRoute` throw a `RangeError`. (Because of R2, `%2e%2e` is a `..` segment and `%2e` is a `.` segment.)
R5. The result starts with `/` and has its segments joined by `/`. It ends with `/` if the original path ends with `/`, or if its last segment is `.` or `..` (after R2); the result of an empty list of segments is just `/`. Otherwise it has no trailing slash.
R6. Letters keep their case, and anything not covered above (including non-ASCII characters and escapes of non-unreserved characters, apart from the hex case) is copied unchanged.
R7. When more than one error applies, R1 is reported before R2's, and R2's before R4's.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

Implement `retrySchedule(options, rand)` in src/retry-schedule.js, as a named export. The stub in that file shows the shape, and test/retry-schedule.test.js shows two examples. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

`retrySchedule` returns the list of waits, in whole milliseconds, before each retry of a failed call.

Rules:
R1. `options` is `{ retries, baseMs, factor, maxMs, jitter }`. `retries` is an integer from 0 to 100, `baseMs` and `maxMs` are finite numbers greater than 0, `factor` is a finite number of 1 or more, and `jitter` is one of the strings `"none"`, `"full"` or `"equal"`. Anything else (including a missing option or an `options` that is not an object) makes `retrySchedule` throw a `TypeError`, except that `baseMs` greater than `maxMs` throws a `RangeError`. A `TypeError` takes priority over the `RangeError`.
R2. The result has `retries` entries: entry `n` (counting from 0) is the wait before retry number `n + 1`. `retries: 0` gives `[]`.
R3. The capped delay for entry `n` is `cap(n) = min(maxMs, baseMs * factor ** n)`, computed in floating point.
R4. With `jitter: "none"` the wait is `cap(n)`. With `"full"` it is `cap(n) * r`, and with `"equal"` it is `cap(n) / 2 + (cap(n) / 2) * r`, where `r` is the next number from `rand()` (a number from 0 up to but not including 1). `rand` is called exactly once per entry, in order, and not at all with `"none"`.
R5. Every wait is rounded to a whole number of milliseconds with `Math.round`, and then is at least 1. (So a computed wait that rounds to 0 becomes 1.)
R6. `rand` must be a function whenever `jitter` is not `"none"` (otherwise a `TypeError`, checked together with R1). If `rand` returns something that is not a finite number from 0 up to but not including 1, `retrySchedule` throws a `RangeError`. `options` and its values are never changed.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

# inventory

A small in-memory stock library: `import { Inventory } from "./src/inventory.js"`.

Rules:
R1. A SKU is trimmed of whitespace at both ends and upper-cased. Every method that takes a SKU does this first, so `" ab-1 "` and `"AB-1"` are the same SKU. A SKU that is not a string, or is empty after trimming, throws a `TypeError`.
R2. A quantity must be a positive integer, otherwise the method throws a `RangeError`. This applies to `add`, `remove`, `reserve` and `release`.
R3. `add(sku, qty)` increases the stock on hand.
R4. `reserve(sku, qty)` sets stock aside. A reservation may be at most what is available (on hand minus already reserved); a bigger one, or one for a SKU that was never added, throws a `RangeError` and changes nothing.
R5. `release(sku, qty)` undoes reservations. It cannot release more than is reserved for that SKU, otherwise it throws a `RangeError` and changes nothing.
R6. `remove(sku, qty)` takes stock away. Reserved stock cannot be removed: the stock on hand cannot go below what is reserved, otherwise `remove` throws a `RangeError` and changes nothing.
R7. `snapshot()` returns an array of `{ sku, onHand, reserved, available }`, sorted by `sku` in plain code-unit order (the order of the `<` operator, not locale order). A SKU with nothing on hand and nothing reserved is left out.

# report

Turns CSV text into a totals report. `parseCsv` (src/csv.js) reads the text, `groupTotals` (src/aggregate.js) adds up amounts by key, and `renderReport` (src/report.js) prints the result.

Rules:
R1. `parseCsvLine(line)` returns the fields of one line as an array of strings. Fields are separated by commas. An unquoted field has the spaces and tabs at both ends removed. A field whose first character, after any spaces and tabs, is `"` is quoted: it runs to the closing `"`, a comma inside it is ordinary text, `""` inside it means one `"` character, and its content is kept exactly (no trimming). After the closing quote only spaces and tabs may come before the next comma or the end of the line, otherwise it throws a `SyntaxError`; a quoted field with no closing quote also throws a `SyntaxError`. An empty line gives `[""]`, and a trailing comma gives a final empty field.
R2. `parseCsv(text)` throws a `TypeError` if `text` is not a string. It splits `text` into lines at `\n` or `\r\n`, ignores lines that are completely empty, takes the first remaining line as the header, and turns each later line into an object keyed by the header fields. A line with a different number of fields than the header throws a `RangeError` whose message contains `line N`, where N is the 1-based line number in the original text, counting the empty lines too. Text with no header gives `[]`.
R3. `groupTotals(rows, keyField, valueField)` adds up `row[valueField]` for each distinct `row[keyField]`. A value must be a string of the form `12`, `-12`, `12.5` or `12.50` (at most two decimals), and a key must be a string; anything else throws a `TypeError`. The sums are exact, in whole cents, and the result is an array of `{ key, cents }`.
R4. The result of `groupTotals` is sorted by `cents` from highest to lowest, ties by `key` in plain code-unit order (the order of `<`).
R5. `renderReport(totals)` takes the result of `groupTotals` (a non-array throws a `TypeError`) and returns one string. Each entry is a line `KEY | AMOUNT`, where the key is padded on the right with spaces to the key width, and the amount is the cents written with thousands separators and exactly two decimals (`123456` is `1,234.56`, `-5` is `-0.05`), padded on the left with spaces to the amount width. After the entries comes a line of `-` characters as long as the entry lines, then a line `TOTAL | AMOUNT` laid out the same way, whose amount is the sum of all the cents. The key width is the length of the longest key, or 5 (the length of `TOTAL`) if that is larger. The amount width is the length of the widest amount, including the total's. The lines are joined with `\n` with no `\n` at the end. For an empty list the output is the dashes line and the total line only.

src/client.js is a small HTTP client wrapper. Add response caching to it, following the rules below, without breaking what it already does. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

`createClient({ fetchImpl, now, ttlMs })` returns `{ get, clear, stats }`. `fetchImpl(url)` returns a promise of `{ status, body }`, and `now()` returns the current time in milliseconds.

Rules:
R1. `ttlMs` is an optional option. A missing `ttlMs`, or `undefined`, means `0`. Any other value must be an integer of 0 or more, otherwise `createClient` throws a `RangeError` (that includes `null`, a string and `NaN`). With `ttlMs: 0` nothing is ever stored in the cache.
R2. `get(url)` calls `fetchImpl` with the URL with any `#fragment` removed, and returns `{ status, body }`. A response with a status from 200 to 299 is stored in the cache under the URL without its fragment, stamped with the value of `now()` read right after `fetchImpl` resolves. While `now() - stamp < ttlMs`, a call to `get` for the same URL (fragment ignored) returns the stored response and does not call `fetchImpl`. At `now() - stamp >= ttlMs` the entry is expired: it is removed and the URL is fetched again.
R3. A response with any other status is returned but never stored. If `fetchImpl` rejects, `get` rejects with the same error and nothing is stored.
R4. While a fetch for a URL is in progress, other calls to `get` for the same URL (fragment ignored) wait for that fetch and get its result (or its rejection) instead of starting another one. This holds whatever `ttlMs` is. Once the fetch has finished, the next call starts afresh.
R5. `get(url, { fresh: true })` never reads the cache and never waits for a fetch already in progress: it always calls `fetchImpl`. If the response is a 2xx one it replaces the stored entry (when `ttlMs > 0`); otherwise the stored entry is left alone.
R6. `clear(url)` removes the stored entry for that URL (fragment ignored), and `clear()` with no argument removes every entry. Neither affects fetches in progress or the statistics. `stats()` returns a new object `{ hits, misses, fetches }`: `hits` counts the calls of `get` answered from the cache, `misses` counts every other call of `get` that got past the URL check (including `fresh` calls and calls that waited for a fetch in progress), and `fetches` counts the calls made to `fetchImpl`.
R7. A response returned by `get` is a deep copy: changing anything inside it, at any depth (its `status`, its `body`, or anything within the `body`), must not change what is stored or what any other caller received, including callers that shared the same fetch. The URL check from before stays: a `url` that is not a non-empty string throws a `TypeError` (as a rejected promise, since `get` is async).

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done

src/config.js loads a JSON config file. Add support for an `extends` key to it, following the rules below, without breaking what it already does. Run the tests with: node --test. Do not change any file under test/.

`loadConfig(file, { readFile })` returns the config object for `file`. `readFile(path)` is given in the options and returns the text of the file (it throws if the file is missing). All paths use `/` and are handled with `node:path/posix`.

Rules:
R1. A config may have an `extends` key: a string, or an array of strings, naming other config files. A name that starts with `/` is used as it is; any other name is relative to the directory of the file that contains it. Every path is normalized with `path.posix.normalize` before it is read or compared, the top-level `file` too, and `readFile` is called with the normalized path. Only a missing `extends` key means no bases. If the key is present with any other value (`null`, a number, an object, `true`, or an array that holds anything other than strings), `loadConfig` throws a `TypeError` whose message contains the path of the file it is in. An empty array is allowed and means no bases.
R2. The result is built by starting with an empty object, merging each base file's result in the order listed (a later one overrides an earlier one), and then merging the file's own keys on top. A base file's own `extends` is resolved the same way, so the process is recursive. The `extends` key itself is not part of the result.
R3. Merging: when both sides of a key are plain objects (not arrays, not `null`) they are merged key by key with the same rules; in every other case the later value replaces the earlier one completely. Arrays are replaced, not joined, and a later `null` replaces an earlier value.
R4. A file that, directly or through its bases, extends itself makes `loadConfig` throw a `RangeError` whose message contains `cycle` and the chain of normalized paths joined with ` -> `, ending with the path that closed the loop (for example `cycle: /a.json -> /b.json -> /a.json`). Reaching the same file twice by different routes (a diamond) is not a cycle.
R5. A file whose text is not valid JSON throws a `SyntaxError` whose message contains that file's path. A file whose JSON is not an object (an array, a string, `null`, and so on) throws a `TypeError` whose message contains its path, as before. This applies to base files too. An error thrown by `readFile` is passed on unchanged.
R6. Each file is read at most once in one call to `loadConfig`, even if several files extend it.
R7. A key named `__proto__` in a JSON file is an ordinary key: it is kept as an own property of the result, at any depth, and is merged like any other key (R3). Loading never changes `Object.prototype` or any other prototype, and the result and every object inside it still have `Object.prototype` as their prototype.

When all the rules hold, reply with the single word: done
